```{r setup}
library(controlcompR)
```

## Minimal realizations

Uncontrollable or unobservable states do not affect the input-output
behavior. `ctrl_minreal()` removes them with orthogonal staircase
reductions:

```{r}
sys <- ctrl_ss(diag(c(-1, -2, -3)), c(1, 1, 0), c(1, 0, 1))
ctrl_minreal(sys)
```

## Hankel singular values

The Hankel singular values \(\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i(W_c W_o)}\) measure
how much each state of a balanced realization contributes to the
input-output map. They are invariant under state transformations:

```{r}
set.seed(4)
A <- -diag(c(0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100)) +
  matrix(rnorm(64, sd = 0.3), 8)
B <- matrix(rnorm(8), 8)
C <- matrix(rnorm(8), 1)
big <- ctrl_ss(A, B, C)
ctrl_is_stable(big)
hsv <- ctrl_hsvd(big)
signif(hsv, 3)
plot(hsv, log = "y", type = "b", ylab = "Hankel singular value")
```

They are computed from Cholesky factors of the two Gramians obtained
directly with Hammarling's method, without forming the Gramians. This
matters when a direction is weakly controllable but strongly observable:
here the realization is a rotated, badly scaled copy of \(I/(s+1)\), whose
Gramians have eigenvalues spanning 16 orders of magnitude, yet the two
Hankel singular values are exactly 0.5:

```{r}
U <- matrix(c(1, 1, -1, 1), 2) / sqrt(2)
Gr <- ctrl_ss(-diag(2), U %*% diag(c(1e4, 1e-4)), diag(c(1e-4, 1e4)) %*% t(U))
ctrl_hsvd(Gr)
ctrl_norm(Gr, "2")
```

`ctrl_balreal()` returns the balanced realization itself, in which both
Gramians equal the diagonal matrix of Hankel singular values. It checks
that the realization reproduces the transfer function:

```{r}
bal <- ctrl_balreal(Gr)
attr(bal, "hsv")
round(ctrl_dcgain(bal), 6)
```

## Balanced truncation

Truncating the balanced realization to order \(r\) keeps the stable
dominant dynamics and gives the a priori error bound
\[
\|G - G_r\|_\infty \le 2 \sum_{i > r} \sigma_i .
\]

```{r}
red <- ctrl_balred(big, order = 3)
attr(red, "error_bound")
err <- ctrl_norm(big - red, "inf")
c(actual = as.numeric(err), bound = attr(red, "error_bound"))
```

The actual error is below the bound, as the theory guarantees. The bound
is also checked numerically: against the error sampled on a frequency
grid and against the H-infinity norm of the error system.
`bound_status` is `"certified"` when that norm computation gave a finite
upper bound below the returned bound, and `"estimated"` when it was not
available (samples alone cannot exclude a larger error between grid
points). A reduction whose own samples contradict its bound raises an
error.

```{r}
attr(red, "bound_status")
attr(red, "error_norm")
```

`method = "matchdc"` (singular perturbation) preserves the DC gain
instead of high-frequency accuracy:

```{r}
red_dc <- ctrl_balred(big, order = 3, method = "matchdc")
c(full = ctrl_dcgain(big), truncate = ctrl_dcgain(red), matchdc = ctrl_dcgain(red_dc))
```

## Comparing responses

```{r}
w <- 10^seq(-2, 3, length.out = 300)
mag <- function(s) 20 * log10(Mod(ctrl_freqresp(s, w)$response[1, 1, ]))
df <- data.frame(w = rep(w, 3), dB = c(mag(big), mag(red), mag(red_dc)),
                 model = rep(c("full (8)", "truncate (3)", "matchdc (3)"),
                             each = length(w)))
ggplot2::ggplot(df, ggplot2::aes(w, dB, color = model)) + ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::scale_x_log10() + ggplot2::theme_bw()
```

## Unstable models

Balanced truncation is defined for stable models. For unstable models the
package separates the stable and unstable parts with `ctrl_stabsep()`,
reduces the stable part and keeps the unstable part exactly:

```{r}
unst <- ctrl_ss(as.matrix(Matrix::bdiag(A, matrix(0.5))),
                rbind(B, 1), cbind(C, 1))
parts <- ctrl_stabsep(unst)
ctrl_poles(parts$unstable)
red_u <- ctrl_balred(unst, order = 4)
sort(Re(ctrl_poles(red_u)), decreasing = TRUE)[1]
```
